en.title: The verb to have
en.summary: Have shows possession, relationship and experience, and is also an auxiliary verb.

paragraphs: Have shows possession, relationships, illness and many everyday events. It is also an auxiliary verb, used to form the perfect tenses. As a main verb it has several meanings, and some of them do not mean own: have breakfast, have a shower, have a good time.

The present is have, but has for he, she and it. In British English have got is also common for possession: I've got a car. For questions and negatives with the main verb, use do: Do you have time? I don't have time. Have got makes its own questions: Have you got time?

paragraphs: When have means eat, drink, take or experience, it needs do in questions and negatives and can be in the continuous: She is having lunch. When it means own, it is not used in the continuous.
Have to means must. It is a modal expression: I have to go. The negative don't have to means it is not necessary. This is different from must not, which means it is forbidden.

items: Wrong: **She have a dog.** Right: **She has a dog.**
Wrong: **I am having a car.** Right: **I have a car.**
Wrong: **Have you time?** (rare in speech) Right: **Do you have time?**

ro.title: Verbul „a avea”
ro.summary: Verbul „a avea” exprimă posesia și are forme diferite pentru fiecare persoană la timpul prezent.

paragraphs: Verbul „a avea” arată posesia sau o relație de familie. Folosim acest verb și pentru a spune vârsta. Pronumele personal nu este obligatoriu.
Verbul „a avea” își schimbă forma pentru fiecare persoană. Pentru negație, punem cuvântul „nu” în fața verbului. Întrebarea se formează doar prin intonația vocii.
